posts.quote: A RESIDENT ASKED FOR EASTER AND PASSOVER. THE CITY REFUSED, SHE SAYS. NOW THE MAYOR IS BEING SUED.
posts.alt: Portrait photo of Dearborn, Michigan Mayor Abdullah Hammoud in a dark suit and light blue shirt. Text below reads: A resident asked for Easter and Passover. The city refused, she says. Now the mayor is being sued.
posts.caption:
A journalist is suing the mayor of Dearborn, Michigan, over how the city treats religious holidays.

Margot Cleveland, a legal commentator who lives in Dearborn, filed the federal suit on September 17 with the American Freedom Law Center. Records from her public-records request show the city spent about $1,500 on "Ramadan Kareem" banners and about $5,000 on a crescent-moon display in a city park. The police department also sold Ramadan shirts bearing its official emblem. The suit names both the city and the mayor and asks a court to order equal treatment.

On April 6, 2025, she emailed the city attorney and asked whether Easter and Passover would get the same recognition. The suit says she never got an answer. In February 2026, the city added crescent-and-star lights to street lights for Ramadan.

She is not asking Dearborn to take anything down. She is asking for equal treatment.
posts.first:
The suit also quotes Mayor Abdullah Hammoud at a City Council meeting, responding to a Christian pastor who objected to a street renaming. Hammoud called the pastor "a bigot" and said: "although you live here, I want you to know as mayor, you are not welcome here."

The city rejects the claims. Dearborn says it has a "longstanding commitment to serving all residents fairly and equitably, regardless of faith or background."

These are allegations in a complaint, and a court has not ruled on any of them.

With the holiday season here, the question is a simple one. If a city pays for banners and displays for one faith's holy month, what does it owe residents of other faiths who ask for the same?

posts.quote: MICHIGAN'S NEW SENATOR ASKED, “WHAT IF” WE REPLACE THE RIGHT TO BEAR ARMS WITH HEALTH CARE? ON JULY 4TH: “FIREWORKS SUCK!”
posts.alt: Photo of Abdul El-Sayed speaking at a Senate committee hearing table, in a blue suit with a microphone in front of him. Text below reads: Michigan's new senator asked, "What if" we replace the right to bear arms with health care? On July 4th: "Fireworks suck!"
posts.caption:
Michigan's new senator-elect once said fireworks "suck" and asked what it would look like to trade a constitutional right for health care.

CNN reported in August that Abdul El-Sayed had made old YouTube videos private. In a now-removed video from July 2024, he says, "Fireworks suck!" and asks viewers to find another way to celebrate the Fourth of July. He cited air quality, the chemicals in fireworks, veterans with PTSD, and pets.

In a video posted April 6, 2023, he said: "What if we tweaked the Constitution, amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have health care?"

El-Sayed, a former Michigan health official who ran as a progressive, beat Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, according to CBS News. He had narrowly won the August 4 primary over Rep. Haley Stevens.
posts.first:
Here is how his campaign answered. A spokeswoman told Fox News: "Abdul respects the Second Amendment, and also believes that access to healthcare is a right." The campaign also said: "Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don't reflect his beliefs today," and pointed to a 2025 post encouraging followers to enjoy fireworks on the Fourth.

To be exact about what he said, he did not call for abolishing the holiday. He asked people to celebrate another way. On the Second Amendment, he floated a rewrite, phrased as a question.

What matters now is how he votes. A senator who says he respects the Second Amendment will have plenty of chances to show it on gun bills.

posts.quote: WISCONSIN'S EDUCATION DEPARTMENT ADJUSTED TEST SCORES TO MASK DECLINES, A STATE AUDIT FINDS.
posts.alt: Portrait photo of Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly, smiling, with short gray hair and glasses, in a blue jacket outdoors. Text below reads: Wisconsin's education department adjusted test scores to mask declines, a state audit finds.
posts.caption:
A new state audit says Wisconsin's education department changed how school test scores were reported, and kept every school from showing a decline.

The nonpartisan Legislative Audit Bureau released its report on November 20. It found that after the Forward Exam's cut scores changed, the Department of Public Instruction set each school's 2023-24 achievement score so it could not fall below the previous year. In the audit's words, "no school or school district's student achievement score for school year 2023-2024 decreased from the previous year, regardless of performance."

The report came out the same week DPI published new report cards rating 95 percent of districts as meeting expectations or better.

Educators recommended new cut scores. DPI then raised about a third of them and lowered about a third. The audit says DPI had no written policy for changing cut scores.
posts.first:
The numbers behind it: DPI expected to substitute the prior year's score for 63.8 percent of schools in English and 44.1 percent in math. Even under the new cut scores, dozens of schools were projected to drop, and DPI said it did not check whether those were real declines.

The audit also says the cut-score meetings were not publicly noticed. DPI cited confidential test questions, and the auditors said no state law lets that override open meetings rules.

State Superintendent Jill Underly called the audit "partisan political theater" and said its points "are all incorrect." Republican Sen. Eric Wimberger, who co-chairs the audit committee, said DPI "cooked the books." That is his charge, not the auditors' wording.

posts.quote: WILLIAM SMALL TO PHILADELPHIA CITY COUNCIL: "We're about to be the super minority."
posts.alt: Photo of a man at a podium during a Philadelphia City Council public comment session. A quote card below reads: William Small, Philadelphia City Council: "We're about to be the super minority."
posts.caption:
At a Philadelphia City Council public-comment session in mid-November, activist William Small warned council members about illegal immigration and Black voters.

"We're about to be the super minority," Small said. He told the council that "blackity black stuff that we love" is "about to go bye-bye, because you guys are ushering in a whole new voter bloc."

Small is a Republican and a majority inspector of elections in Philadelphia's 59th Ward. He has appeared before the council before and has had heated exchanges during public testimony, according to the Philadelphia Tribune.

His argument is about the future. Immigrants who are in the country illegally cannot vote, but those who become citizens over time can. Townhall's summary says he asked how the council would treat Black voters once that happens, and where residents who are already here fall on the council's priority list.
posts.first:
The clip has spread across social media since November 20, and Townhall reported on it.

The context is a city that has gone far on immigration. In April, the council passed a package of bills limiting how federal immigration agents can operate in Philadelphia.

Small's point is a political one: that the city's leaders are working for newcomers while residents who are already there, especially Black residents, are being left behind. Whether you agree with him or not, he said it to the council's face, on the record.

We did not find a response from council members to his remarks. We used only the phrases that match across several transcripts of the video.
